🇷🇺 THE STEADILY GROWING AUTHORITY OF BRICS 🇷🇺

*Exclusive  by @SMO_VZ 

President Vladimir Putin told the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi that the authority and influence of BRICS in the world is steadily growing. That statement was not a slogan. It was a description of a shift already visible in trade, energy, technology, and diplomacy.

 "BRICS now covers about a third of the Earth’s surface, accounts for roughly 40 percent of global GDP, and is home to nearly half of humanity. Its partnership is built on equality, good-neighbourliness, and mutual consideration of interests. Those principles stand in contrast to a system that, for decades, served a narrow group of countries."

The New Delhi session was titled “Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism.” Putin treated that theme as the central task of the age. The world is living through geopolitical, geoeconomic, technological, and social transformation. Lifestyles, healthcare, the environment, the structure of society, and the demographic map are all changing. 

In that landscape, BRICS has established itself as a key centre of global governance. The future of international politics, security, the economy, and humanitarian cooperation will depend, in large measure, on the collective decisions of its members. 🇷🇺🌍

THE UNIPOLAR SYSTEM IS BECOMING A THING OF THE PAST

The unipolar system of international relations, which served the interests of a narrow group of countries, is gradually becoming a thing of the past. The global balance of power is shifting towards new centres of growth in the Global South and East. More and more states are openly asserting their determination to defend their national interests and to take part in addressing global challenges.

That is not a prediction. It is an accounting of output, population, manufacturing, energy, and political will. The old hierarchy assumed that a small circle of capitals could set the rules and expect the rest of the world to adapt. That assumption no longer matches the distribution of real capacity. Emerging markets are no longer the periphery of someone else’s system. They are the engines of growth. BRICS did not invent that fact. It organised around it. 🇷🇺

RESISTANCE FROM THOSE WHO THINK IN COLONIAL CATEGORIES

The formation of a multipolar world is not proceeding without difficulties. It meets resistance from those who remain accustomed to thinking in colonial terms, dividing the world into a flourishing garden and a wild jungle, and seeking to prosper at the expense of others. Unwilling to accept the new realities, they use every means at their disposal to hold back emerging competitors.

Those methods include tariff wars, illegitimate sanctions, economic pressure and blackmail, interference in the internal affairs of sovereign states, and the direct use of force.

 Existing hotbeds of tension are deliberately fuelled. New conflicts and divisions are provoked. The result is that the entire system of international relations malfunctions, and multilateral institutions lose effectiveness.

The garden-and-jungle image is not decorative. It names a habit of mind: one part of the world is treated as civilised and entitled to set terms; the other is treated as raw material, a security problem, or a market to be managed. Putin’s point was that this habit cannot survive the redistribution of power now under way. 

Countries that have spent years being lectured about “rules” while watching those rules applied selectively will not accept the lecture as law. 🇷🇺⚔️

THE UNITED NATIONS AND THE CHARTER AS THE SOURCE OF LAW

Against that backdrop, Russia considers it particularly important to preserve and strengthen the United Nations’ central role in world affairs. The UN Charter remains the cornerstone of international law, even as some countries attempt to replace it with a so-called “rules-based order” whose rules were written by no one knows whom.

Putin called for expanding the UN Security Council to include greater representation from Asia, Africa, and Latin America. The Council still reflects the world of 1945 more than the world of 2026. A body that claims to keep the peace cannot remain legitimate if entire continents that now drive growth and population have no permanent voice at the table. Reform is not a gift to be granted by the old permanent members. It is a condition of the institution’s own survival.

THE NEED TO REFORM THE IMF, THE WORLD BANK AND THE WTO

The need to improve the system of global economic governance has long been evident. The International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, and the World Trade Organisation were created in very different political and economic realities. They are finding it increasingly difficult to adapt to a world in which economic activity is steadily shifting towards emerging markets.

These institutions remain platforms for dialogue among leading economies. Coordination among BRICS countries inside them therefore matters. During Russia’s 2024 BRICS chairmanship, a dedicated consultation mechanism on WTO-related issues was established. That is the practical method: use the existing rooms while building the capacity to set new rules where the old rooms no longer work.

Simply modernising yesterday’s institutions is no longer enough. Entirely new sectors have appeared — the platform economy, financial technologies, and digital trade. Each requires its own institutions and regulatory frameworks. BRICS can take a leading role in shaping them. China, Russia, and other members were among the founding participants of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation established in Shanghai. That is one example of writing the next rulebook instead of waiting to be written into someone else’s. 🇷🇺💡

RUSSIAN INITIATIVES INSIDE BRICS

Putin put several concrete Russian proposals on the table: payment, settlement, and depository infrastructure within BRICS; a new investment platform; a reinsurance mechanism; and a grain exchange. These are not abstractions. They are answers to a specific vulnerability. When reserves can be frozen and banks can be cut from settlement networks, sovereignty becomes a technical problem as well as a political one.

The business community has already shown strong interest. The BRICS Business Forum produced a range of initiatives for practical cooperation. Ambitious multilateral projects are being planned. The political statements and the commercial projects are two sides of the same effort: reduce exposure to a single currency, a single messaging system, and a single set of sanctions levers. 🇷🇺🏦

Other OPINIONS  on BRICS  & RUSSIA:

JEFFREY SACHS ON THE MULTIPOLAR AND MULTI-CURRENCY WORLD

Economist Jeffrey Sachs has argued for years that the unipolar moment is over and that global institutions must catch up with the actual distribution of output. He has pointed out that BRICS countries now produce a larger share of world output than the G7 when measured in purchasing-power terms, and that emerging and developing economies are projected to grow faster than high-income countries for years to come.

Sachs has called for a UN that reflects the Global South, including a permanent Security Council seat for India and a broader voice for Asia, Africa, and Latin America. He has said the United States share of world output is no longer what it was when the postwar architecture was frozen in place, and that China is already a larger economy on a purchasing-power basis. In that setting, he argues, the BRICS countries need representation and voice in setting the rules.

On finance, Sachs has been explicit. The world is moving not only to a multipolar order but to a multi-currency order. He has described a future IMF that cannot function if one country continues to call the shots, and he has urged BRICS to move forward, in practical terms, on monetary and financial cooperation and on local-currency payments. Ahead of the New Delhi summit he listed greater financial cooperation and local-currency settlement among the tests of whether the grouping was serious.

Sachs has also warned that threats aimed at punishing countries for reducing dollar dependence can accelerate the very diversification they are meant to stop. India–Russia trade, including energy, is already being settled outside the dollar system in growing volume. China is expanding the use of the renminbi. The technology for a multicurrency payments framework, he has said, already exists. The political will is what is being tested. His argument aligns with Putin’s institutional agenda: reform the old bodies, and build parallel rails where reform is blocked. 🌍

JOHN MEARSHEIMER AND THE LOGIC OF GREAT-POWER AUTONOMY

John Mearsheimer approaches the same facts from offensive realism. He has said the United States, China, and Russia have all been great powers since around 2017, which means the world has already been multipolar. The United States remains the most powerful of the three, China is a peer competitor translating economic weight into military power, and Russia is the weakest of the three great powers — but still a great power. In that system, liberal hegemony gives way to balance-of-power politics.

Mearsheimer’s relevance to BRICS is structural. Rising great powers do not accept permanent dependence on a rival’s financial weapon. Russia learned that when reserves were frozen and banks were expelled from Western settlement systems. China understands that the same arsenal could be used in a Taiwan contingency. Great powers therefore build their own institutions. The Belt and Road Initiative, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, and BRICS are examples of that pattern.

Commentaries associated with Mearsheimer’s line of argument have stressed a further point that matches the New Delhi agenda. BRICS is not, in the first instance, trying to mint a single replacement for the dollar overnight. It is building something more threatening to dollar privilege: payment infrastructure that allows nations to trade without touching the American financial system. That is exactly the logic of Putin’s call for BRICS payment, settlement, and depository infrastructure. Dependence on a rival’s clearing house is not a technical inconvenience. It is a strategic vulnerability. Realists expect great powers to close that vulnerability. 🇷🇺🇨🇳

WHAT “GENUINE MULTIPOLARITY” ACTUALLY REQUIRES

Putin closed by saying the main goal of the joint work of the BRICS countries is to improve the efficiency of global governance and to ensure genuine multipolarity and justice in world affairs. Genuine multipolarity is not a slogan about many flags in a photograph. It means that no single capital can freeze another country’s reserves, dictate its payment rails, or rewrite international law as a private “rules-based order.”

It also means that new sectors — platforms, fintech, digital trade, artificial intelligence — will not be regulated solely by the jurisdictions that happened to write the last generation of standards. BRICS members possess enormous intellectual and technological potential. That potential is the association’s substantial advantage. Using it to write the next generation of rules is the difference between being a forum and being a centre of governance.

The New Delhi Declaration and the surrounding work on local-currency trade, interoperable payment systems, and the New Development Bank’s local-currency financing sit inside that larger project. Members still differ on pace and on how far to go toward a common currency. The direction of travel is not mysterious: more settlement in national currencies, more links among national payment systems, more capacity to move goods, grain, energy, and capital without a veto from outside the group. 🇷🇺

CONCLUSION

RUSSIA ALONG WITH CHINA ARE THE JOINT KINGPIN LEADERS OF THE BRICS COMMUNITY. 

They bring complementary strengths: Russia’s energy, commodities, military weight, and experience under the heaviest sanctions regime ever assembled; China’s industrial scale, technology, financial infrastructure, and capacity to organise trade corridors across Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Together they give the grouping a spine that no other pair of members can supply.

Their dedication is not hidden. It is written into the proposals for a BRICS payment and settlement system, a new investment platform, a reinsurance mechanism, and a grain exchange. It is written into the surge of ruble–yuan settlement. It is written into the argument that the UN Charter, not an informal “rules-based order,” remains the source of international law. It is written into the demand that the IMF, the World Bank, and the WTO stop treating emerging markets as junior partners in a house designed in 1944.

The purpose of that work is to remove Russia, China, and their partners from the sanctions lever and from the trading power of the US dollar. Sanctions and dollar clearing were built as instruments of discipline.

 A multipolar order that still runs through those instruments is not multipolar. It is unipolarity with extra chairs. BRICS, with Russia and China as its joint kingpins, is building the alternative rails — political, institutional, and financial — so that sovereignty does not depend on permission from a single currency and a single set of correspondent banks.

The unipolar garden is no longer the whole map. The rest of the world is not a jungle waiting to be civilised. It is a set of centres of growth that intend to set their own terms. That is the meaning of Putin’s New Delhi speech, and that is the direction in which Sachs’s institutional reforms and Mearsheimer’s great-power logic both point. 🇷🇺🇨🇳🌍

It has become fashionable these days to abuse IITs and their faculties. I get it, freedom of speech, healthy skepticism of institutions, all fair game. 

But before that fashionable takedown becomes the whole story, sit with this 1 fact for a second....

Right now, last month, IIT profs have put more free, peer-reviewed, university grade course content into the world than any other institution on the planet, and most Indians have never watched a single hour of it.

2001....

A handful of IIT directors come back from a trip to Carnegie Mellon, having seen an American prof build an entire functioning university around teaching people online. 

They are stunned enough to try replicating it for India, in engineering, at a scale nobody had attempted before.

The idea finally took shape under Atal Bihari Vajpayee's government. The man holding the HRD portfolio through that entire stretch, 1998-2004, was Murli Manohar Joshi, himself a physics prof before he was ever a minister. 

On January 26, 2003, months before NPTEL's own official rollout that year, Joshi Ji personally inaugurated a companion initiative, the Eklavya Technology Channel, explicitly built to beam actual IIT classrooms into homes across the country. 

7 IITs and the IISc quietly went live. 

No press conference most people remember. Just profs, cameras, and a govt that wrote the check for something nobody could fully prove would work.

The word "MOOC" did not even exist yet. Coursera and edX launched in 2012. 

The term was not even coined until 2008. NPTEL was already recording real lectures years before Silicon Valley invented free online university education and got magazine covers for it. 

India did not copy the MOOC revolution, it built one of the first drafts before anyone had a name for it.

Fast forward to now. 

NPTEL is the largest repository of engineering and science course content on Earth: 

- 56,000+ hours of lectures

-3,200+ courses

- a YouTube channel with 1.86B views and 5.6M subscribers

...built entirely by government-funded faculty, not a venture-backed edtech company. 

Not entertainment.... 

Thermodynamics. Signal processing. Soil mechanics. Quantum Mechanics. 

Built by profs people love to mock as "out of touch," "irrelevant," "stuck in an old system."

A student in rural Bihar with a smartphone has, right now, the same lecture an IIT KGP student sat through, free, no JEE rank required. 

And yet ask most students outside the IIT system if they have done a single NPTEL certification, and you will mostly get silence. 

Employers still do not weight it the way they weight a foreign MOOC certificate with a fraction of the rigor. The exact students this was built for often do not know it exists.

If a country builds the largest free reservoir of elite education on the planet, a decade ahead of everyone else, and barely drinks from it, is that the institution's failure / ours, for criticizing loudly and never once checking what is already free and sitting right there?

Criticize the IITs all you want, no institution should be above scrutiny. But this particular story deserves the same volume as the criticism. It just never gets it.

FREE SPEECH DOESN’T NEED A GOVERNMENT PERMISSION SLIP.

The Modi Government’s growing agenda for controlling what Indians can see, read, post, critique and challenge online should concern every citizen — regardless of political affiliation.

From demanding takedowns to tightening the time available to platforms to scrutinise government notices, the direction is unmistakable: comply first, question later. India’s 2026 IT-rule changes cut the takedown window for unlawful content to just three hours, while the Government has also proposed making certain official advisories legally binding on platforms. (Reuters⁠)

That is precisely why Elon Musk’s decision to resist, scrutinise and challenge government demands rather than blindly obey every request matters.

X’s own stated policy is that requests can be challenged when they are legally defective, overly broad or appear to impermissibly burden freedom of expression. (Transparency⁠)

And that is where the real problem begins for the Modi Government.

When an independent platform refuses to become an obedient extension of the State, the State’s attempts to control the narrative become visible.

No algorithm can hide that.
No press conference can spin that.
No amount of propaganda can erase that.

If the Government’s demands are genuinely about protecting citizens and enforcing legitimate law, let them withstand public scrutiny, judicial scrutiny and independent platform scrutiny.

But if criticism, dissent, inconvenient facts and uncomfortable questions are increasingly treated as “content to be removed”, then Musk’s resistance does something far more important than defending X.

It exposes this Govt’s vile intent and its surreptitious machinery.

And once the machinery is exposed, the Modi Government stands increasingly bare before the very citizens whose freedom of expression it claims to protect.

A democracy doesn’t become stronger by silencing criticism.
It becomes stronger by surviving it. 

There seems to be a crackdown on Modi Govt these days from every corner and every cross section of India. Are “Acche Din” finally around the corner for India ⁉️

@TeamYouTube this situation has gone way beyond a normal enforcement issue. On July 28, my channel started receiving an unusual wave of privacy complaints. Within roughly 3 days, 40+ complaints were filed against 41 completely unrelated videos, and 31 videos were removed. I appealed multiple removals and repeatedly contacted YouTube Support and Legal, but I never received a clear, case-specific explanation of the alleged privacy violations.

Then on August 14, the entire channel was terminated for Impersonation. I appealed and was rejected. When I contacted Creator Support, I was first told the termination was for Spam, despite the termination notice clearly stating Impersonation. The case was escalated, and I was then told the internal review confirmed Impersonation. I repeatedly asked a simple question: Who or what did I supposedly impersonate, and what exactly on the channel violated the policy? No specific answer was provided.

I submitted another official appeal through Google Form. It was confirmed as received and sent for specialized review, but that appeal has now also been rejected for Impersonation.

So after multiple reviews, I still haven't been told what specific person, channel, branding, video, or conduct supposedly constituted impersonation. I have never intentionally impersonated anyone or claimed to represent another creator or entity.

The matter is now pending before GAC in India and has also been brought to @SFLCin.

I am not asking for special treatment. I am asking for a fair, evidence-based review and a clear explanation of what actually happened. Please escalate this properly and reconsider the termination. @YouTube @UpdatesFromYT @YouTubeCreators @YouTubeIndia

Ray-Ban Meta glasses struck again. A woman walking home alone was secretly recorded by a man who approached her, then posted the footage on Instagram alongside similar clips of him doing this to other women, as part of "pickup" content.

She's filed a police complaint for stalking and voyeurism. IFF is assisting her with a legal notice to the creator, Instagram, and Meta, the second such notice against Meta in India.

This isn't a one off. It's a design problem.
Read more about it: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

A woman was followed, stopped on a dark street, secretly recorded through Ray-Ban Meta glasses and turned into an Instagram “pickup” reel that reached over 23 lakh views. Now, our legal notice seeks accountability from both him and Meta. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

The legal notice therefore puts Meta on notice not merely as the platform hosting the video, but as the designer, developer, manufacturer, marketer and seller of the glasses. It alleges negligence and product liability, arguing that Meta knew about the pattern of misuse but continued selling the device without an effective way for non-users or people being recorded to report that misuse. (9/10)

The notice seeks removal of every copy, preservation and disclosure of evidence, suspension of monetisation, an account of profits, an apology, and ₹2.05 crore in compensatory and exemplary damages. This case raises a larger question: when a company makes a camera that can be worn like ordinary glasses, who protects the person being recorded? Privacy cannot depend on whether the person being filmed has an Instagram account. (10/10)

The Supreme Court has closed India's Got Latent cases, but the question of an “Influencer Code” is not entirely over. On 14 August 2026, the Court quashed all FIRs arising from the episode and left the “larger issues” of regulating online speech for “another appropriate case”. Here is what that means. (1/7)

Read More: https://t.co/hecp2rl9W4

That qualifier matters. Executive action restricting speech must have a legal basis consistent with Article 19. The Court has previously held that executive instructions cannot independently impose restrictions on fundamental rights. The signed order also contains no finding that the content in question was obscene, nor does it establish a new standard for online speech. (6/7)

For now, there are no guidelines and no pending judicial direction requiring them. But MIB can still attempt regulatory changes, including through amendments to the IT Rules. If it does, IFF will insist on the public consultation promised to the Supreme Court, compliance with the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy and meaningful participation by affected creators and users. (7/7)

NIXI has changed its justification for suspending chalosansad dot in yet again. After first citing a “critical keyword”, and then relying on a 2004 policy clause that did not apply, it now invokes the Emblems Act and demands Central Government permission within seven days. On 8 September, IFF wrote back seeking a standstill and answers. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/2grOxR1bMy

The timing matters. The domain was suspended on 22 July. NIXI’s new legal opinion was obtained on 29 August, more than a month later and only after we challenged its earlier reasons. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that administrative action must stand or fall on the reasons given when the decision was made; authorities cannot ordinarily supplement an order with new reasons after it is challenged. (6/7)

NIXI has now also said that six other .in domains containing “Sansad”, along with other domains containing “Sansad”, “Parliament” or cognate expressions, will be examined. On 8 September, we asked NIXI for a 48-hour standstill on de-registration, deletion, transfer or reallocation of chalosansad dot in, confirmation of Aadhaar deletion, and disclosure of the correspondence it says raised concerns about publication. If no standstill is given, the registrant will approach the court. (7/7)

Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

NIXI has also given the registrant seven days to produce Central Government permission. Yet its reply identifies no ministry, officer, form, fee, procedure or timeline through which such permission can actually be obtained. We have therefore asked NIXI to explain the legal basis for this demand, and to provide the legal opinion dated 29 August on which its new position relies. (5/7)
Our government suppresses dissent by criminalizing criticism

quotedTweet.text:
On September 10th, 2013, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act, a vague law that was being used to arrest people for simply expressing dissent online.

11 years later, Maharashtra wants to bring it back in a new form, by amending the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for "online criminal defamation." But defamation is already covered under Section 356 of the BNS, and civil remedies already exist.

So why does the police need this new power? Recent FIRs against citizens and influencers for calling out potholes and infrastructure failures may hold the answer. We've fought this battle before. We don't need a new 66A with a new number.

text:
A 2:01-minute reel documenting villagers’ concerns over the proposed Google data centre in Visakhapatnam was blocked in India for 111 days. On 10 September 2026, it quietly came back online. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/TVxhdw9ZA1

The Sahyog route also raises a serious constitutional concern. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because the blocking framework contained procedural safeguards, including notice, hearing and a reasoned order. Section 79(3)(b), meanwhile, was read down to require a court order or government notification. A system that blocks first and explains nothing is difficult to reconcile with those safeguards. (9/10)

The reel is back, and we welcome that. But the questions remain unanswered, Who ordered the blocking? Why did the order name an unrelated person? Was a periodic review conducted? Why was the reel restored? IFF will continue seeking these answers from Andhra Pradesh authorities. Journalists should not need months of litigation to learn why their public-interest reporting was censored. (10/10)
